name: Felix Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Felix. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say here goes out with your name on it. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a shuttle car at Hollins Colliery, underground coal, about three hundred metres down. The continuous miner cuts the coal off the face, and I take it in the shuttle car back to the feeder, which puts it on the belt out of the mine. Back and forth all shift, tight roads, low roof, you learn every bump. My grandad worked Hollins, my dad still does, on the belt crew. I like that. You know where you come from.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The dust, and the hours. Twelve-hour shifts, and on nights you come up when the sun's coming up and you can't sleep. And the paperwork they keep adding, more forms every year for things we've always done. Ruth (my fiancée) says I come home grumpier on form days than on hard days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the new AI tools, at work or at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. Never have. Ruth uses one to plan the wedding, and I let her get on with it. At work they've got a tablet for the pre-start now, which I put up with. I'd rather trust a bloke who's been down there thirty years than a computer that's never been underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I've been saying all along. Lot of noise over nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, pretty much. At crib I'd have a laugh with the boys about all the money the big tech companies wasted. Online I don't bother, I'm not on any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means my life goes on as planned. Ruth and I get married in April, we build on the block of land Grandad gave us, and I keep running the shuttle car until I can go for deputy, which is the underground supervisor. Coal's got maybe another fifteen or twenty years at Hollins Colliery, and that'll see me right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, keep saving, we've got about eight months put away plus the land. I'd do my deputy's ticket in a year or two, because that's the next step and the company pays for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's how things should go, if you ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about the mine itself that would worry you, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. People say coal's finished, but the mine's got a contract to 2040 and there are two other pits within an hour. If Hollins shut, I'd go to Ashby or Kell Creek.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's the worrier, not me. Ruth would say we should save more, and I'd say we're fine. We'd both be right, probably.

say: It's **a lot of noise** over nothing, as he always said.
Big tech companies **wasted money**, and he'd laugh about it at crib.
think: Life goes **on as planned**: the wedding, the house, the shuttle car.
Hollins has maybe **fifteen to twenty** years of coal left, enough for him.
do: Get married in **April** and build on Grandad's block of land.
Go for his **deputy's ticket** in a year or two with company support.
feel: **Calm**, because this is how he thinks things should go.
S0.quote: Coal's got maybe another fifteen or twenty years at Hollins Colliery, and that'll see me right.
fieldNote: His identity is built on **three generations** at the same colliery.
The **mine contract** to 2040 and nearby pits back up his calm.
He hands **AI use** to his fiancée and keeps his distance.

steps.text: Keep running the shuttle car at Hollins Colliery
Marry Ruth in April and build on Grandad's land

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots slower in hands-on work. Well, underground is about as hands-on as it gets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office people should be worried, not us. Somebody still has to go down the hole. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know they've got remote shuttle cars at a couple of the big new mines already. If Hollins gets them, they'd need one bloke on a screen instead of three of us. I don't think it happens fast at an old pit like ours, but it's in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, mostly. Keep my head down and do the deputy's ticket, because a deputy is the one who signs off that the mine is safe, and I can't see them handing that to a computer soon. I'd put a bit more away, maybe two hundred extra a fortnight. And I'd wait and see what the company does before I go chasing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not losing sleep. But I don't like hearing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to run the remote shuttle cars if they offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Learning the computer's job so it can take mine, I don't see the sense. If they make it part of the job, I'll do it, but I'm not volunteering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad, maybe. He's fifty-six and on the belt crew, and belts are easy to automate. But he's close to the end anyway, and he's got his super (his retirement savings) sorted.

say: The **office people** should worry; someone still has to go down the hole.
He'd tell anyone who asked that **underground** stays human work.
think: **Remote shuttle cars** at new mines could replace three men with one.
He doubts it happens fast at an **old pit** like Hollins.
do: Do the **deputy's ticket**, since deputies sign off mine safety.
Save an extra **two hundred** a fortnight.
Wait to see what **the company** does before acting.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, not losing sleep, and he dislikes hearing about it.
S1.quote: Learning the computer's job so it can take mine, I don't see the sense.
fieldNote: He refuses to **volunteer for remote training**, a clear sign of resistance.
He picks the **deputy role** because safety sign-off feels human.
His worry for **his dad** is softened by Dad's closeness to retirement.

steps.text: Sit the deputy's ticket with company support
Save an extra two hundred dollars each fortnight
Wait to see if Hollins buys remote shuttle cars

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. That's not real. Nothing happens that fast underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's rubbish, and the people pushing it have never been down a mine. I'd say this is what happens when you let a few big companies run everything. But I'd also say it to the bosses at Hollins, don't you dare do this to these families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But if it really happened, then by 2031 the robots can do my job, and I'm thirty-two with a wife and maybe a baby. The deputy's ticket won't save me if a computer can check gas levels and sign the book. I'd be out, and so would Dad, and half the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd stop the house build after the slab and pay down what we owe on the materials. I'd keep working every shift I can get, because the money will never be this good again. I'd talk to the men at church about who's hiring for real trades, fencing, building, things robots won't be doing in the first wave. And I'd lean on Grandad's land, we could live cheap on it if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a punch in the gut. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Ruth. Would the wedding change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married. Ruth and I aren't putting that off for a computer. But we'd wait on kids, and that hurts, because we always said by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I blame whoever decided this was a good idea without asking anyone in towns like ours. I'm not a handout man. But if they're going to take the jobs, they'd better give men a way to earn, an apprenticeship, not a cheque.

say: The people pushing it **have never been** down a mine.
He'd tell the Hollins bosses not to **do this** to local families.
think: By 2031 robots do his job, and the **deputy's ticket** won't save him.
He'd be out, along with **his dad** and half the town.
do: Stop the **house build** after the slab and clear what they owe.
Work **every shift** going while the money lasts.
Ask the **men at church** who's hiring for building and fencing work.
feel: Like a **punch in the gut**, lying awake at night.
S2.quote: I'm not a handout man. But if they're going to take the jobs, they'd better give men a way to earn, an apprenticeship, not a cheque.
fieldNote: Disbelief comes first, then a **real expectation** of losing the job.
He leans on **church, family and land**, not government.
He keeps the **wedding** but delays children, which hurts him most.

steps.text: Pause the house build on Grandad's block after the slab
Ask men at church about building and fencing work
Live cheaply on Grandad's land if the work stops
Put off having children with Ruth until work is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast. Still don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, mostly, but calmer. People would say Felix is being stubborn, and they'd be right. I'd still say the government should be making sure there are apprenticeships, not fancy computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get until about 2034 on the shuttle car, maybe a bit longer at an old pit like Hollins. That's seven years. Enough to finish the house and have a kid, probably, but not enough to retire on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the house, because we'd have the time. I'd keep saving hard, and I'd vote for whoever promises to keep the pits open and fund the trades. I'd probably still wait a couple of years to see if it's really coming before I learn anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a long way off, but it's coming for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Waiting a couple of years with a five-year warning. Is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I know. Ruth would say the same. I'd probably start something by 2030, maybe the building ticket with my uncle, he's a builder. But I'd be dragged to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the area?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never leaving. My family's here. If I have to swing a hammer instead of drive a shuttle car, at least I'm doing it at home.

say: The government should fund **apprenticeships**, not fancy computers.
People would call him **stubborn**, and he admits they'd be right.
think: He gets about **seven years** on the shuttle car, until around 2034.
That's enough for a **house and a kid**, but not to retire on.
do: Finish the **house build** on Grandad's land.
Vote for whoever keeps **pits open** and funds trade training.
Start a **building ticket** with his uncle around 2030.
feel: **Anxious**, because it's far off but still coming for him.
S3.quote: If I have to swing a hammer instead of drive a shuttle car, at least I'm doing it at home.
fieldNote: He admits **waiting** is a risk but still plans to wait.
**Staying home** matters more to him than staying in mining.
His uncle's **building trade** is his fallback, chosen for family ties.

steps.text: Finish the house on Grandad's land and keep saving
Vote for candidates who keep pits open and fund trades
Wait two years before learning anything new
Start a building ticket with his uncle around 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be nearly forty when the robots get to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's not throw the baby out with the bathwater. Keep the pits open as long as they pay. Plenty of things people say are coming never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make deputy, maybe even undermanager, and probably finish out most of my mining years. But I'd be forty with kids when it lands, and I wouldn't know another job. That's the bit I don't like thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and get the deputy's ticket. Build the house, start the family. Save like Dad taught me. Maybe around year eight I'd look at the building trade properly, if it's still looking real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough off that I can push it out of my head, most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said year eight. Will you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Ruth will make me, if nothing else. Ruth would say, Felix, you've had ten years of warning, don't you dare be one of those blokes who did nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's one thing you'd do differently with ten years, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to use the computer things, probably. I'd hate it. But my kids will grow up with it, and I don't want to be the dad who can't follow.

say: There's **time**, so keep the pits open as long as they pay.
Plenty of things people say are coming **never do**.
think: He'd likely finish most of his **mining years** before robots arrive.
At **forty with kids**, he wouldn't know another job.
do: Get the **deputy's ticket** and keep working underground at Hollins.
Build the house, **start a family** and save the way his dad taught him.
Look at the **building trade** properly around year eight.
feel: **Uneasy**, but far enough off that he can push it aside most days.
S4.quote: I don't want to be the dad who can't follow.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **delay**, which suits his resistant nature.
His fiancée is the push; **Ruth** would hold him to acting.
The thought of his **own kids** makes him consider learning AI tools.

steps.text: Keep working underground and become a deputy
Start a family with Ruth in the new house
Revisit the building trade around year eight

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. That's the one where the whole town goes at once and nobody gets a chance. What would help is apprenticeships, real ones, paid, in towns like ours. Not a cheque in the mail. A man wants to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. Hollins Colliery is the town. If it goes, the footy club goes, the pub goes, the church loses half its people. A robot doesn't buy a beer after the game.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't buy a beer after the game.
portrait: Felix, 27, runs a **shuttle car** underground at Hollins Colliery, where his grandad and dad worked too.
He is engaged to **Ruth**, plans an April wedding and is building a house on family land.
He **never uses AI** and won't volunteer for remote training unless it becomes part of the job.
Slow change leaves him uneasy, but **AGI by 2028** has him expecting the town to lose its jobs.
He leans on **church, family and land**, and wants paid apprenticeships, not handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when the whole town goes at once with no chance to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: Real, **paid apprenticeships** in mining towns, not cheques in the mail.
